text: Forty minutes until Ruth's review, and I have already printed the slides twice. I stand at the window of the fourth-floor meeting room, watching the grey rain move across the car park toward the building. My pen taps the table in a rhythm I cannot stop.

The quarterly numbers are on the screen behind Dev, and he has not yet clicked to the last page. I keep my eyes on the cursor as it hovers over the next slide, counting the seconds between each slow scroll. Somewhere down the corridor a printer starts up and runs for a long time.

The email from Human Resources arrived at 4:55, and the subject line is only the word Meeting. I open the calendar invite and see my manager's name in the organiser field, plus a room number I have never booked. I shut the laptop lid halfway and then open it again, reading the time slot a third time.

Tomorrow the audit team arrives and will go through every folder on the shared drive. I sit in the empty kitchen, watching the coffee machine drip into the pot, and I make a list of files to check before then. The list runs past the bottom of the page and onto the back.

The oven timer reads six minutes and the dinner guests are already at the door, stamping snow from their boots. I lift the lid on the pot and see the sauce has split into a thin oily ring around the edge. I stand there with the wooden spoon while the bell rings again.

The cake has been in the oven for forty minutes, and the middle still wobbles when I tap the tin. Through the glass I watch the top begin to darken at one edge, slowly, like a stain spreading over paper. I turn the dial down by a notch and wait, my oven glove still resting on the door handle.

The food critic's booking is at seven, and the first plate has to leave the kitchen in ten minutes. I wipe the rim of a white bowl for the third time, watching the sauce skin over under the heat lamp. Behind the swing door the dining room gets louder with every table that sits down.

Every fork in the drawer has a bent tine, so I open the cutlery tray and find the last clean spoon. Dinner is set for six and my father always arrives early, so I can already hear his car turning into the lane. I lift the lasagne from the oven and watch the cheese sink in the middle.

The rain has not stopped since the motorway junction, and the wipers are dragging a smear across the windscreen. Ahead the brake lights of the lorry in front come on in a red line, and the traffic bunches up behind it. I ease my foot off the accelerator and watch the gap between us shrink, not yet sure how fast the queue is coming.

The instructor has not said a word since the roundabout, and her pen rests on the clipboard on her knee. We are nearing the last junction on the test route, the one where the examiner marks everything. My hands stay at ten and two as the junction sign comes into view above the hedge.

The ticket inspector is working down the carriage one row at a time, and I can see the grey of her uniform between the seats. My season pass expired on Friday and sits folded in my coat pocket, under the receipt for the coffee. I keep my face toward the window and feel the train slow for the next station.

The school run is over and the car is empty except for a crushed juice carton under the passenger seat. I am parked outside the garage where the MOT test was booked for three, and the mechanic has just come out wiping his hands on a rag. He walks toward my window slowly, and I already know from his face which way this will go.

Along the moor path the grass is flattened by wind, and the sky to the west has gone a flat, heavy grey. I stop at the stile and look back at the valley, where the first curtain of rain is sliding over the far farm. My boots are still wet from the stream, and I start walking faster toward the trees.

The tide has turned while I was reading on the sand, and the water is already sliding across the flat towards my towel. I gather the bag and the flask, watching a line of foam come in over the ripples at the edge of the beach. Down at the far end, the lifeguard's whistle sounds once across the bay.

The warden in the green jacket is working along the row of pitches with a clipboard, stopping at each tent to peer at the number on the post. I am still crouched at the guy ropes, my fingers numb, and our pitch is the next one along. Behind me the stream runs loud over the stones, and the last of the light is already going.

Snow has been falling on the pass since noon, and the gate at the car park is due to close at four. I walk down the switchbacks with my poles clicking on the stones, watching the cloud thicken over the ridge behind me. Each bend shows more of it pouring over the col toward the path.

The flood water has crept under the cupboard door, and the grey towels I laid along the skirting are already dark through. I kneel on the lino and press a corner of the rug down, feeling the damp soak up into my knee. Upstairs the ceiling over the bath has a brown ring that wasn't there at breakfast.

The landlord's inspection is booked for ten, and the letter on the mat says he will check the boiler and the smoke alarms. I scrub the hob with a sponge, then go over the same stubborn patch around the tap, which will not come off. The cooker clock reads 9:41 and the van pulls up outside.

The hallway smells of wet dog and the tumble dryer has stopped mid-cycle. My mother-in-law's car has just turned into the close, and I can see her hat through the front window. I shove a basket of unfolded shirts under the stairs and pull the sofa cushions straight, one at a time.

The pile of letters on the bureau has grown since Tuesday, and the red envelope from the council sits on top with its window facing up. I hold the gas bill in one hand and the tea towel in the other. Each dish I rinse at the sink takes a little longer, because I keep glancing at the post.

The results letter from the clinic arrived this morning, and I have not opened it yet. It sits on the kitchen table beside the fruit bowl, the clinic logo facing up each time I walk past. The nurse said the answer would come by Friday, and today is only Tuesday.

The dentist's drill has been running in the next room for ten minutes, and the sound comes through the wall in short whines. I lie back in the chair and stare at the light above me, my jaw already aching from the clamp. The hygienist sets down a tray of steel tools with a clink, and the assistant says the dentist will be in shortly.

The blood pressure cuff tightens around my arm and the nurse's eyes drop to the dial. She writes a number on the chart, then writes another, and says nothing while the pen moves. I watch her hand, the cuff hissing as it lets go, and wait for the doctor's door to open down the corridor.

The scan is scheduled for ten past two, and the radiology corridor smells of disinfectant and warm plastic. My name is on a screen above the desk, and the queue ahead has shrunk to one man with a crutch. I fold the paper gown over my arm and stand by the door, listening for the technician to call.

My sister's text lights up the phone on the bedside table: she is coming to stay for the weekend, and she says we need to talk about Dad. I read it twice in the dark, then put the phone face down on the sheet. Through the wall I can hear the neighbour's television, a laugh track, rising and falling.

The car is already in the drive when I get home, which means Mum has come early again. Through the front window I see her coat over the arm of the armchair and two suitcases by the stairs. I stop on the step with my key in my hand, knowing she has been waiting in the kitchen since noon.

The gate buzzer goes at seven, and I know who it is from the long pressed ring. It is my uncle, the one who has not spoken to us since the funeral. I lift the lid of the biscuit tin, put it back, and smooth the tablecloth where the coffee rings have dried.

Dinner is in an hour and my daughter has not come down from her room since the call from school. I stand at the foot of the stairs with a tea towel over my shoulder, listening to the faint thump of music through the ceiling. When her door finally opens, I will have to say what the head teacher wrote.

The exam hall is quiet except for the scrape of chairs and the wall clock ticking over the door. The invigilator walks down the row between the desks, pausing beside each candidate. I have three questions left on the paper and ten minutes, and her shoes stop at the end of my row.

The seminar leader has printed the marks on a single sheet, and the stack is face down on the lectern. Round the room people fold their hands and wait for their names. My essay, handed in twenty minutes past the deadline, is somewhere in the pile, and the leader lifts the first sheet.

The lab report is due at nine, and the results table on my laptop still has three blank columns. I refresh the spreadsheet and watch the cell for the final run flicker, then turn to the bench where the sample tubes sit in their rack. The supervisor's bag is already by the door, and she is pulling on her coat.

The results of the nursing practical go up on the corridor wall at nine, and the crowd around the board is already three deep. I hang back with my bag on one shoulder, watching students push forward and then fall back. My name is on the list somewhere in the middle of the second page.

The race starts in four minutes, and the crowd along the barrier is three deep. I bounce on my toes at the back of the pack, feeling the cold tarmac through my thin trainers. The hill I walked yesterday rises ahead of us, its top lost in a low grey cloud that is sliding closer to the course.

The pool attendant has the whistle in her mouth and the lane ropes are being pulled taut across the deep end. I stand on the edge in my swimsuit, toes curled over the tiles, watching the timer on the wall flick toward the hour. The coach taps his stopwatch and points at the lane nearest the diving board.

The gym's treadmill beeps and the trainer walks over, glancing at the number on the screen. Tomorrow is the fitness assessment, and my first run this morning ended with me clutching the rail. I lift my foot onto the belt again, my breath loud in my ears, and watch the pace dial creep up.

The starter raises her arm at the far end of the track, and the lane lines blur as the others lean forward. Last month I came last in this meet, and the runners beside me remember it. I dig my spikes into the rubber and wait for the crack of the gun.

The bride's mother rings the bell at eleven, and the dress is still on the dummy in the back room. I thread the needle a third time, my hand unsteady on the silk, and watch the thin stitch pull against the seam. Along the hem, the pins I set last night have dropped onto the floorboards, and the hall is already filling with voices.

The bicycle chain has jumped off the cog twice on the hill, and the mechanic's shop closes at five. I tip the bike onto its saddle in the shed, turning the pedal by hand while the grease smears up my wrist. Outside, the sky over the allotments is going the colour of ash, and a gust rattles the corrugated roof harder each time.

The kiln cooled overnight and the door is open now, so I can see the rows of pots on the shelves. Two of the glazed rims have hairline cracks, and the café owner is coming at ten to collect the whole order. I lift the first pot to the window and turn it slowly, looking for the next one.

The walnut table I have been sanding for a week shows a dark crack along one leg, the kind the glue cannot close. The client is due at five to collect it, and her van is already rounding the corner. I run my thumb along the split and feel the grain lift under my nail.

The queue at the post office snakes past the lottery stand, and the clerk has only just called number forty-two. I hold my parcel against my chest with the registered slip folded inside my raincoat. Behind the glass a man is shaking his head at someone's form, and the slow tap of his stamp carries across the room.

The self-checkout light is blinking red above lane three, and the attendant is already walking toward it with a scanner in his hand. My basket holds the bread, the milk and a bag of rice, and the total on the screen has been stuck for a full minute. I stand with my card half out of the reader and wait for the beep.

The bank's letter says the direct debit failed, and the card machine at the till has just declined my payment for the second time. The woman behind me shifts her basket to the other arm and sighs at the queue. I slide the card in again, slowly, and watch the small grey screen ask me to wait.

The security guard has stopped beside the exit, and his eyes follow each shopper through the gate. A jar of olives is still in my jacket from the aisle, and the receipt in my hand shows only the bread and milk. I step toward the gate, and the panel above it gives a soft click.

The connecting flight in Madrid left without us, and the rebooking desk here has a line of forty people. I stand at the end of it with my boarding pass creased from the last gate and the suitcase handle pressing into my palm. Above the counter the screen cycles through new departure times, each one later than the last.

The ferry's engines have started to thrum through the deck, and the captain's voice on the speaker says the crossing will be rough past the headland. I grip the rail by the stairwell and watch the grey swell lift the boat toward the wall of waves ahead. Below me a child is being sick into a paper bag.

The hotel receptionist has my passport open on the counter and is reading the expiry date twice. Outside the revolving door, a taxi is idling with its meter running, and the driver has stopped looking at his phone. I hear her say that the visa on the form does not match, and I start to unzip my bag.

The train from the airport is pulling in slowly, and the station clock says the last connection leaves in six minutes. I haul my case down the steps, feeling the wheels catch on each stone edge. At the barrier the ticket gate flashes red, and the guard at the end of the platform is already raising his flag.

The choir director has tapped her baton twice, and the altos are shuffling their folders to the right page. My solo starts after the next four bars, and my music has a smudge of water across the top line. I hold the paper steady in both hands and watch the baton lift for the count.

The critic from the Sunday paper has reached the third room, and she is taking notes at each canvas for longer than the last. My painting hangs on the far wall, the last one before the door, its varnish still wet where I touched it up at dawn. I pull my sleeve down over my wrist and follow her steps toward it.

The pottery class ends in twenty minutes, and the teacher has begun walking around the wheels, checking each bowl with the flat of her hand. I have pulled the clay too thin again, and the wall of mine is wobbling as it turns. I let my foot off the pedal and watch the rim sag slowly toward the table.

The audition panel sits behind a folding table in the church hall, and the pianist is already flexing her fingers above the keys. Three names are left on the sheet in front of me, and mine is the last. I tune the fiddle once more and feel the wood dig into my jaw.

The upload bar has stopped at ninety-seven percent, and the deadline for the grant portal is at midnight. I refresh the page and the spinning wheel comes back, tiny and patient. On the other screen a notification slides in from the bank, then another from the portal, both with the same red dot.

The phone buzzes on the desk with a number I don't recognise, and then a second call comes straight after it. The voicemail icon has been climbing since morning, and the last message was from the solicitor's office. I turn the phone over, read the first line of the notification, and let it keep buzzing against the keyboard.

The software update has been pending since Monday, and the laptop now shows a warning that it will restart in five minutes whether I save or not. I have forty open tabs and an unsaved draft of the proposal, and the cursor blinks in the middle of a half-finished sentence. Outside the window, the office lights go off one floor at a time.

The video call is set to start at four, and the client's name has just appeared in the waiting room list. My camera shows a grey wall behind me and a stray hair at the edge of the frame. I unmute the microphone, hear the soft tone of his arrival, and wait for his face to fill the screen.
